newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan moves to ease concerns about rising yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan moves to ease concerns about rising yen.

text.p: Japan's most influential currency official acted on Tuesday to stave off speculation about the rising yen, saying Tokyo has not changed its foreign exchange policy despite its growing trade surplus with the United States.
The dollar rose nearly a yen on Tuesday morning on the comments by Eisuke Sakakibara that there has been no change in the Minister of Finance's (MOF) foreign exchange policy.
"The MOF's forex policy has not changed," said Sakakibara, who has been dubbed "Mr Yen" because of his influence over currency markets.
"As with the U.S. Treasury, (the MOF) does not have any intention at all of using foreign exchange rates as an instrument of trade policy," Sakakibara told Reuters.
Sakakibara's appointment as vice minister of international affairs at the Ministry of Finance is expected to be formally approved by Japan's cabinet on July 15.

Currently director-general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, Sakakibara was widely seen as the key figure in driving the dollar back above 100 yen in 1995 after it hit a postwar low of just under 80 yen in April of that year.
His comments came amid growing speculation that Japan might allow the yen to float higher as a means to help trim its rising trade surplus and avoid friction with Washington.

Sakakibara's remarks caught traders off guard, forcing them to unwind dollar short positions built up after a report on Monday showed that Japan's trade surplus in the first 20 days of June more than doubled from the same period last year.

"His comments made it clear that (the ministry) will not put upward pressure on the yen," said Masao Yoshikawa, senior manager of the international treasury department at the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd.
The dollar rose as high as 113.45 yen following Sakakibara's remarks, up from around 112.50 yen before the comments were reported.
The dollar had fallen as low as about 112.05 yen in early European dealings on Monday, its lowest level in nearly a month.

Dealers said the talking-down of the yen by Sakakibara was also aimed at preventing the stock market from falling, because any falls would hurt the weak economic recovery and financial institutions struggling to get rid of bad assets.

The ministry "could be worried that a sharp rise in the yen would hurt the already fragile stock market and have a negative impact on the economy", said Kazunori Iida, manager of the foreign exchange department at trading firm Nissho Iwai Corp.
The Tokyo bourse's key Nikkei average closed slightly higher on Tuesday at 19,853.89, but was still well below its recent high of about 20,910 set on June 26.
A senior bank dealer at a top Japanese bank said: "If the dollar sinks sharply below 110 yen, that will cause serious problems for some Japanese investors."
Japanese institutional investors have invested heavily in foreign bonds and stocks in the past two years, apparently with little regard for the currency risks involved.
Any further failures among Japanese financial institutions would increase worries about the institutions and dampen business sentiment.

Dealers said, however, that the bias towards a higher yen will not be reversed anytime soon and that overwhelming dollar-selling demand by Japanese exporters and investors could persist for the time being.
This could cap the dollar at 114.50 yen, they said.
"I think the dollar's fall below 110 yen is only a matter of time," said Nissho Iwai's Iida. "As more time passes, more dollar-sell positions are accumulated," he said.

The release of Japan's May current account data, due out on Wednesday, and any comments from a Japan-U.S. Business Council meeting in San Francisco that started on Monday are expected to favour yen buying, dealers said. The current account is the broadest measure of trade in goods and services.
Ko Haruki, chief dealer at Midland Bank Plc, said the MOF "may have wanted to have a cushion before these yen-boosting events".
